h1: A project report for a non-alcoholic drinks plant
title: Non-Alcoholic Drinks Plant Report | Craft Beer School
desc: What a project report for a non-alcoholic drinks plant must show: line capacity, shelf life, water, packaging cost and distributor credit.
teaser: No excise licence does not mean no risk. The cash sits in packaging, water and credit.
standfirst: A non-alcoholic drinks plant faces different questions from a brewery: line speed, shelf life, packaging cost and how long distributors take to pay. The report must answer them with numbers.
sections:
Soft drinks, juices, ready-to-drink tea, kombucha, hop water and non-alcoholic beer share a customer, a shelf and a cold chain, but they differ from beer in ways that change the project. There is no alcohol licence route, which removes one risk. The product is usually lower-priced and higher-volume, so margins per unit are thin and the plant must run efficiently. Check with the regulator which food safety registration and other approvals apply to your product in your state or country. Rules differ and change.

Where alcohol is restricted, a non-alcoholic plant may be the only option. Local law comes first.
Line capacity is a chain, too

Capacity in a bottling or canning plant is set by the slowest machine and by how much of the time the line runs. A hypothetical in neutral units: a filler rated at 3,000 bottles an hour, 8 hours a day, 250 days a year gives 6 million bottles. Real lines lose time to changeovers, cleaning, stoppages and supply gaps. At 70 percent overall equipment effectiveness, output is about 4.2 million bottles a year.

The same logic applies upstream and downstream: water treatment, blending, pasteurising or aseptic filling, labelling, packing, palletising. See capacity planning in a project report.
Process choice: hot fill, tunnel pasteurise or aseptic

The route to a stable product sets the plant and the cost. Products with low acidity or live cultures need different treatment from acidic juices. Hot fill, tunnel pasteurising and aseptic filling each have different equipment, energy, pack and shelf life implications. State the shelf life you need for your distribution route and the process that gets you there. A product that must reach shops two months away needs a shelf life that matches.

Soft drink plants use water as an ingredient and for rinsing, cleaning and cooling. Put a number on water per litre of product and on the treatment plant. A plant on borewell water may need softening or reverse osmosis. That adds to both capex and running cost. Sugary rinse water raises the load on effluent treatment. Check discharge rules locally.

Packaging is often the largest cost. A hypothetical bottle sells to the distributor for 20 units. Liquid costs 4, packaging 6, labour and energy 3 and freight 2. That is 15, leaving 5, or 25 percent, before overheads and marketing. A 10 percent rise in packaging cost, 0.6 units, takes about 12 percent off that margin. Packaging prices swing with raw materials, so test them. See sensitivity analysis for a drinks project.

Soft drink sales go through distributors and retailers on credit. If you sell 100 units a month and wait 45 days for payment, about 150 units are outstanding at any time. Add stock of packaging and finished goods. This can be a larger funding need than the plant. Show it as a line in the cash flow and state the credit terms you assume, with evidence from the distributors you have talked to.

A drink that spoils on the shelf costs far more than the batch. Yeast, mould or secondary fermentation in a sweet product can swell a pack and send it back. The report should name the control points: ingredient testing, filling hygiene, pasteurising or aseptic records and retained samples. It should also say how you would trace and recall a batch. A lender will not expect a perfect record, but they will want to see that you have thought about it and costed the laboratory.

The shelf is crowded and the major brands have scale. The report should show a clear place for your product: a flavour, a positioning you can support, a local fruit or a price point. Make no health claims you cannot prove. Follow local labelling rules. Build volume from your outlets, as described in the market section of a project report.

Finish with the same financial package as any project: projections, debt cover, NPV, IRR and payback. No report can promise a loan. It can show the logic.
faqs: Is a non-alcoholic plant simpler to license?
It avoids the alcohol licensing route, but food safety, pollution and other approvals still apply. Rules differ by country and, in India, by state. They also change.
What is the biggest cost in a soft drinks plant?
Often packaging, followed by the liquid ingredients and logistics. Model it carefully and test its price.
Why is working capital so large?
Because distributors pay on credit and you hold packaging and finished stock. The plant is only part of the funding need.
Can the same plant make several drinks?
Sometimes, if the process and line allow. State what changeovers and cleaning the report assumes.
